title: Size-4 numerators are PROVED in F_q[T]: F_4[T] with A=T, F_2[T] with A=T²
connection: The two function-field analogues whose numerator has the same norm as 4 (|A| = 4: q=4,deg A=1 and q=2,deg A=2) are theorems (FUNCTIONFIELD_ES Thm 6.1, 6.3), proved by a FINITE congruence covering. Over Z a finite covering is impossible (Mordell square classes).
why: Pinning down exactly which Z-obstruction each FF proof dodges isolates the one ingredient Z lacks; it is the cleanest 'proved twin' of ES.

title: Char-2 cancellation ↔ signed ES with a size-controlled negative term
connection: In char 2 two monic denominators of equal minimal degree cancel at ∞ (m = 2), which is what the F₂ identities exploit. Over Z the closest mechanism is 1/x − 1/x' with x' ≈ x, i.e. signed ES where the negative term is tiny.
why: If the F₂ identities lift to signed integer identities whose sign defect is confined to a small term, the remaining task is a 'sign repair' problem, which is a different and more concrete integer statement.
first_step: Lift the F₂[T] identity of Thm 6.1 coefficientwise to Z[T] (T ↦ integer), record which term goes negative, and measure its size relative to 4/n.

title: Rate comparison: FF density-zero failures (Thm 5.3) vs Vaughan's exceptional-set bound
connection: At fixed q the FF failures have density 0 via a one-prime identity plus Dirichlet/RH in F_q[T]; over Z Vaughan gives #exceptions ≤ N exp(−c log^{2/3} N). The FF proof uses RH (Weil), so its rate may be a power saving.
why: A power-saving rate in FF suggests what GRH would buy over Z; a GRH-conditional power-saving ES exceptional bound would be a new (conditional) integer theorem.
first_step: Extract the explicit rate in FUNCTIONFIELD_ES Thm 5.3; then check whether a GRH-conditional ES exceptional-set bound with power saving exists in the literature (search 'Erdős–Straus exceptional set GRH').

title: q→∞ failure (Thm 2.1) ↔ few numerators per prime (Luca–Pappalardi, Mond–Portier A₃(p))
connection: ES_q(A,P) fails for a proportion → 1 of P as q → ∞ with deg P fixed; over Z, Σ_{p≤x} A₃(p) ≍ x(log x)³(up to loglog), so a typical p has only polylog numerators m with m/p a 3-term sum.

first_step: Read Mond–Portier 2201.11805 and check whether the proof shows A₃(p) is supported on m ≤ (log p)^C for most p — if so record the integer 'Thm 2.1'.

title: Sign-subgroup world: positivity = leading coefficient in a subgroup H ≤ F_q^*
connection: Monic (H = 1) is Hayes' choice; H = F_q^* is the trivial sign-free problem. Taking H = squares (index 2) mimics Z, whose sign group {±1} has index 2 in nothing but whose 'positive' half is index 2 in Z∖0.
why: Interpolating H shows whether hardness is controlled by the index of the cone; an index-2 cone FF problem might be the most faithful model of ℕ ⊂ Z.
first_step: Run the existing ffl_* search with leading coefficients restricted to squares for q = 3,5,7, deg P ≤ 8, and compare failure counts to the monic version.

title: Constant numerator 4 fails in char ≥ 5 because leading coefficients are 1,2,3 ↔ 'x > n/4' archimedean bound
connection: Prop 1.2: 4/P with monic denominators fails for every P in char ≥ 5 (sum of three monic reciprocals has leading coefficient 1,2,3). Over Z the analogue is the archimedean bound x ≥ n/4 that makes m ≥ 4 the first hard numerator.
why: It shows that '4 > 3' is the genuine source of hardness; the integer statement 'm ≤ 3 trivial, m = 4 hard' has an exact FF mirror, which supports using FF degree bookkeeping as a model of archimedean size.
first_step: Write the dictionary entry 'leading coefficient count ↔ number of terms ≥ numerator' and check whether k-term m/n with m ≤ k is trivial in both worlds (it is over Z: m/n = Σ 1/n).

title: Large-q monodromy (Bary-Soroker style) for 'divisor of A·C·P+1 in a residue class'
connection: Over F_q[T] with q → ∞, factorization types of P-tied polynomials such as A·C·P + 1 become equidistributed via full symmetric monodromy; ES Type II needs a divisor of 4Cp+1 in class −1 mod 4C over Z.

title: Keating–Rudnick variance in F_q[T] as model for the variance of Type II counts over C
connection: Variance of arithmetic functions in FF arithmetic progressions is computed exactly via random matrix theory for q → ∞. The fixed-p ES count Σ_C #(divisors of 4Cp+1 ≡ −1 mod 4C) is a sum of divisor-in-AP indicators.

title: Positivity at a finite place: cone = polynomials with constant term 1
connection: Replace 'monic' (sign at ∞) by 'X(0) = 1' (sign at the place T). This cone is multiplicatively closed but contains elements arbitrarily close to 1 T-adically, i.e. it is not discrete at its sign place.

title: Genus-1 coordinate rings: ES over F_q[x,y]/(E) with sign at the point at infinity
connection: Drinfeld–Hayes rings with nontrivial class group: a 'prime' P generates a non-principal ideal in general, so 4/P is not even an element unless P is principal; ES becomes a statement about principal primes or ideal classes.

connection: Positivity defines the narrow ray class group mod ∞. For Q it is trivial; for monic F_q[T] the sign group F_q^* contributes. ES-type certificate classes are ray classes; the size of the 'sign part' changes which classes are reachable.

connection: In FF the numerator degree k plays the role of log m. Families with k→∞ at fixed q correspond to m/n problems with growing m (Schinzel), where Vaughan-type density results still hold over Z.

connection: The ultraproduct of F_q[T] over q has a pseudo-finite constant field; ES over it is decided by Lang–Weil point counts on the fixed-degree ES variety, giving failure (Thm 2.1) for standard degree.

title: Mason–Stothers in F_q[T] vs abc over Z for size of largest ES denominator
connection: abc is a theorem in F_q[T] (Mason–Stothers); applied to ES identities it bounds degrees of solutions. Over Z, abc would bound sizes of x,y,z from below/above in terms of rad(xyz·n).

title: Mordell–Schinzel proves ES FALSE over Z[T] (eventual positivity) at P = mT + r²
connection: Over Z[T] with cone 'positive leading coefficient', a solution at P = mT + r² would be a polynomial identity covering a square class, excluded by Mordell–Schinzel. So Z[T] is an analogue world where ES is provably false.
why: It certifies that any proof over Z must be non-uniform in n (cannot come from a single polynomial family per class); Z[T] is the 'false twin' to set against the FF 'true twins'.

title: Which non-square classes (m, r) admit an ES polynomial identity?
connection: Mordell–Schinzel excludes square r mod m. For non-square r, is there always an identity 4/(mT + r) = Σ 1/X_i(T) over Z[T]? Over 840 Mordell finds identities for all non-square classes; for general m this is the polynomial world's version of ES.

connection: Primes p = f(S,T) for a non-principal form f (e.g. disc −23, h = 3) form a non-congruence set. A polynomial identity 4/f(S,T) = Σ 1/X_i(S,T) in Z[S,T] would cover a non-abelian Chebotarev set.

connection: Primes ≡ 1 (mod 4) are exactly the primes S² + T². A Z[S,T] identity valid on a cone would prove ES for the primes in it; Mordell–Schinzel-type obstruction bites at (S,T) with S²+T² a square (Pythagorean pairs).

connection: Over R[T] with positive leading coefficients there is no integrality of coefficients, so ES becomes a semialgebraic condition on the solution variety, like the q → ∞ limit but with an ordered constant field.

world: A. Function fields F_q[T] and polynomial rings

title: ES over Q(T) with denominators in Z[T] but positivity 'for T in an interval' (semi-algebraic cone)
connection: Instead of eventual positivity (lc > 0), require denominators positive on [0, ∞) or on an interval. This cone is not multiplicatively a valuation cone and sits between Z[T]-lc and genuine pointwise positivity.
why: Mordell–Schinzel uses positivity on infinitely many integer points; different positivity notions show exactly how much positivity the obstruction needs.
first_step: Check whether T1 at squares already kills identities whose denominators are positive only for T in a residue class mod M.
world: A. Function fields F_q[T] and polynomial rings

title: FF Thm 6.3 search technique (covering trees) on Z with growing modulus
connection: The computer-assisted FF proofs used a covering tree whose leaves are congruence classes with identities. Over Z the same tree never closes (squares), but its growth rate measures the 'certificate deficit'.
why: The FF/Z comparison of tree growth quantifies the gap; a sub-exponential growth over Z would suggest a growing-family proof is plausible.
first_step: Run the FF covering-tree code verbatim on Z (moduli 840·k) to depth 6 and record the number of open leaves per depth vs the FF case.
world: A. Function fields F_q[T] and polynomial rings

title: F_q[T] with q → ∞ AND deg P → ∞ jointly: the critical scaling deg P ≈ c·q
connection: Thm 2.1 (fails, q→∞ fixed degree) and Thm 5.3 (density-0 failures, fixed q) bound a phase diagram; along deg P ≍ f(q) there is a critical curve.
why: The critical curve is the FF version of 'expected number of solutions ≍ log² p'; its exact location in FF predicts how close Z is to the threshold.
first_step: Compute failure proportions on a grid q ∈ {3,5,7,9,11,13}, deg P ∈ {3..7} and fit the 50%-failure curve.
world: A. Function fields F_q[T] and polynomial rings

title: Artin–Schreier identities in char p: the 'Frobenius twist' certificate family
connection: In char p, X ↦ X^p is additive, so identities like 1/X^p − ... interact with Frobenius; e.g. (P+1)^p = P^p + 1. Certificate families using P^p are unique to char p.
why: A Frobenius-twist family that covers an FF class unreachable otherwise shows a char-p-only mechanism; over Z its only shadow is Fermat's little theorem congruences (power ladders mod p).
first_step: Search char-3 identities where a denominator is (P + c)^3 or P^3 + c and see whether they cover classes the linear families miss.
world: A. Function fields F_q[T] and polynomial rings

title: ES over F_q[T] with the extra condition 'distinct denominators' — equivalent or not?
connection: Over Z, distinctness is (believed/known) harmless for n > 2. In F_q[T] char 3, the trivial 3/P = 1/P+1/P+1/P shows repeats matter; with distinctness the char-3 numerator-3 case becomes non-trivial.
why: A distinctness-sensitive FF world is a new problem whose behaviour in char 3 could mimic Z with numerator 4.
first_step: Check whether 'ES_3(T, P) with distinct monic denominators' fails anywhere for deg P ≤ 8.
world: A. Function fields F_q[T] and polynomial rings

title: ES over F_q[T][1/T] (S-integers in FF) — analogue of Z[1/3]
connection: Inverting a prime T in F_q[T] gives units T^k; the other_rings Lemma 3.1 then supplies universal divisors e | 1 + T^k with e in the 'class 3' analogue, collapsing ES.
why: Confirms the cone-discreteness principle in FF and quantifies how many units are needed (smallest k).
first_step: Find smallest k with a divisor of 1 + T^k in the needed class mod A for q = 3, A = T²+1.
world: A. Function fields F_q[T] and polynomial rings

title: Dirichlet-density version of ES_q: probability that a random monic P of degree n satisfies ES
connection: Rather than all P, compute the exact probability π_q(n) that random P of degree n is ES-good; integer twin is the density of n ≤ N with a 'short' ES solution.
why: Exact π_q(n) as a rational function in q (if it is one) would be a structural prediction for the Z density of 'easy' n by certificate size.
first_step: Compute π_3(n), π_5(n) for n ≤ 8 and test polynomial-in-1/q fits.
world: A. Function fields F_q[T] and polynomial rings

title: Function-field ES with A irreducible vs A reducible (4 = 2·2 is reducible)
connection: 4 = 2² over Z; FF analogues with A = T² (reducible, proved over F₂) vs A irreducible of degree 2. If the reducible case is systematically easier, ES's numerator being a prime square is relevant.
why: Points at whether 4 = 2² structure (square of the dyadic prime) is used by any Z mechanism.
first_step: For q = 3, compare failure sets for A = T² vs A = T² + 1 (irreducible) at deg P ≤ 8.
world: A. Function fields F_q[T] and polynomial rings

title: Function-field Type II ↔ binary quadratic forms over F_q[T] (Artin's imaginary quadratic function fields)
connection: Type II ES data encode representations by binary forms; over F_q[T] with q odd, binary forms have class groups of imaginary quadratic function fields (Artin). Class numbers are given by L-function values (RH known).
why: An FF formula 'ES count at P = combination of class numbers' with RH would give exact asymptotics, whose Z twin is a Dirichlet-class-number formula for ES counts.
first_step: Express the FF Type II count at fixed P as a sum over discriminants of class numbers h(D) and test numerically for q = 3.
world: A. Function fields F_q[T] and polynomial rings

title: Positive ES over Z[1/ℓ] for EVERY odd prime ℓ (unit-sum mechanism; checked ℓ < 3000)
connection: Over Z[1/ℓ] the mechanism of other_rings Lemma 3.1 works iff some 1 + ℓ^k has a prime factor ≡ 3 (mod 4). scripts/z52b_analogues_zl.py: every odd prime ℓ < 3000 has such k ≤ 7 (max at ℓ = 2017). A reciprocity argument shows failure for all odd k would force ℓ ≡ 1 (mod 8).
why: Turns Prop 3.2 (ℓ = 3) into a uniform theorem over all Z[1/ℓ]; the proof (Zsigmondy + reciprocity) records exactly what 'one inverted prime' buys.
first_step: Prove: for ℓ ≡ 1 (mod 8) some odd k has 1+ℓ^k with a prime factor ≡ 3 (mod 4) (try Zsigmondy primitive divisors of ℓ^{2k}−1 with k odd and their classes mod 4).
world: B. S-integers, number rings, cones, non-commutative rings

title: ℓ-adic denominator depth k(p): least k with a positive Z[1/3]-solution having 3-denominators ≤ 3^k
connection: Over Z[1/3] every n has a solution (Prop 3.2, needs 3^3 in a denominator). Define k(p) = least 3-adic depth of a positive solution in Z[1/3]; ES over Z ⇔ k(p) = 0 for all p.
why: Interpolates between a proved world (k unbounded allowed) and ES (k = 0); proving k(p) ≤ 1 or ≤ 2 for all p would be a new intermediate theorem.
first_step: Compute k(p) for primes p ≡ 1 (mod 4) up to 10^6 by searching solutions with denominators in (1/3^k)·Z; look at the distribution of k(p) and whether k(p) ≤ 1 always.
world: B. S-integers, number rings, cones, non-commutative rings

title: Inverting the target prime trivializes ES: positive ES over Z[1/p] for 4/p
connection: In Z[1/p] the unit-sum mechanism applies with ℓ = p itself: if some 1 + p^k has a divisor e ≡ 3 (mod 4) (true for all p < 3000 by the Z[1/ℓ] computation) then 4/p = 1/x + 1/(u p x) + 1/(v p x), x = (p+e)/4. So allowing p-power denominators removes the obstruction; e.g. 4/5 uses e = 3 | 1 + 5.
why: Localizes the difficulty: allowing p-power denominators kills it. A statement 'ES with p-depth bounded by 1' is a tightening hierarchy like k(p).
first_step: Write the explicit identity (minimal k with e | 1 + p^k), then define the 'p-depth' hierarchy and check whether depth-1 (one factor p^{-1} in one denominator) already suffices for all p ≤ 10^6.
world: B. S-integers, number rings, cones, non-commutative rings

title: Smooth-numerator relaxation: 4/p = 1/x + a/y + b/z with a, b B-smooth
connection: Over S-integers with S = {primes ≤ B} ES becomes 'numerators allowed to be S-units'. Over Z this is a relaxation of ES with explicit smooth numerators.
why: For fixed B this might be provable by the unit-sum mechanism with several primes; the minimal B(p) is a new invariant with ES ⇔ B(p) = 1.
first_step: Compute B(p) for p ≤ 10^6: least B such that a solution with B-smooth numerators exists, restricting to small denominators.
world: B. S-integers, number rings, cones, non-commutative rings

title: Real quadratic O_K with N(ε) = −1: positive ES PROVED via inert ℓ ≡ 3 mod 4 and η ≡ −1 mod ℓ
connection: Prop 3.3: a totally positive unit η with ℓ | 1 + η supplies a universal divisor ℓ ≡ 3 (mod 4). Over Z the only units are ±1, so this step has no direct replacement; its integer shadow is a p-independent divisor of a p-tied integer, which only congruence (B1) supplies.
why: This is the proved twin with the most transparent mechanism; any 'unit-like' integer object (e.g. the Pell/unit-orbit families) is a candidate replacement.
first_step: Read UNIT_ORBIT_ES.md for integer replacements of η and list which ones produce divisors of 4Cp+1 independent of p.
world: B. S-integers, number rings, cones, non-commutative rings

title: Trace descent: Galois-sum an O_K solution to get an integer identity with numerator 8
connection: If 4/n = Σ 1/x_i with x_i ∈ O_K (K real quadratic), adding the conjugate equation gives 8/n = Σ Tr(x_i)/N(x_i). When Tr(x_i) | N(x_i) for each i, this is a 3-term unit-fraction representation of 8/n.
why: Turns the proved real-quadratic world into an integer statement for numerator 8 (Schinzel-type), with an explicit divisibility condition to engineer.
first_step: For the D = 2 identity of Prop 3.3, compute Tr and N of each denominator as polynomials in n and check the divisibility Tr | N on residue classes.
world: B. S-integers, number rings, cones, non-commutative rings

title: Norm descent: multiply an O_K solution by its conjugate
connection: From 4/n = Σ1/x_i and 4/n = Σ 1/x_i' (conjugates), the product (Σ1/x_i)(Σ1/x_i') = 16/n² gives 16/n² as a 9-term sum of 1/(x_i x_j'); pairing diagonal terms 1/N(x_i) gives integer unit fractions.
why: Exhibits a route from a proved world to a k-term integer Egyptian representation of 16/n²; probably weaker than ES but a concrete transfer statement.
first_step: Write the 9 terms and check when the off-diagonal pairs x_i x_j' + x_j x_i' combine into integers; test with the D = 2 identity.
world: B. S-integers, number rings, cones, non-commutative rings

title: Gaussian cone ES (Bradford–Ionascu Conj. 1.1) is OPEN — the Z[i] twin of ES
connection: Denominators in Z[i] with Re, Im of equal sign. The cone is discrete at ∞ and has no small units, so the unit-sum mechanism fails, as over Z. The other_rings principle predicts a genuine lottery problem.
why: A second open twin with richer arithmetic (split primes) — progress there (e.g. density-1 results) could be transported.
first_step: Implement a search for the Gaussian cone ES for Gaussian primes of norm ≤ 10^5 and record failures; check whether failures concentrate at squares as over Z.
world: B. S-integers, number rings, cones, non-commutative rings

title: Two-term ES over norm-Euclidean Z[√d] (Bradford–Ionascu Thm 3.1) ↔ divisor ≡ 3 mod 4 criterion
connection: Bradford–Ionascu show even 4/n = 1/a + 1/b holds over Z[√d] for d ∈ {2,3,5,…,73} (no positivity). Over Z, 4/n = 1/a+1/b needs a divisor of n in a class mod 4; in O_K prime splitting supplies more divisors.
why: Identifies the step as 'enough divisors in the right ray class'; the integer replacement is the e-slice divisor condition on a p-tied integer.
first_step: Read §3 of arXiv:1405.4025 to extract the ray-class condition used, then state the Z analogue for 4Cp + 1.
world: B. S-integers, number rings, cones, non-commutative rings

title: Totally positive ES over arbitrary number fields K with an infinite unit group
connection: Generalize Prop 3.3: if K has a totally positive unit η and a prime ℓ ≡ 3 (mod 4) (rational, inert or split suitably) with η ≡ −1 (mod some prime above ℓ), positive ES holds for rational n. Conjecture: true for every K with unit rank ≥ 1 and a totally positive unit of infinite order.
why: Would show the Z difficulty is exactly 'unit rank 0 + discreteness', i.e. Q and imaginary quadratic fields are the only hard worlds among number fields.
first_step: Try K = Q(√3) (N(ε) = +1) and a cubic field with mixed-sign units; search η^j ≡ −1 mod ℓ numerically (other_rings evidence covers D = 3, 6, 7).
world: B. S-integers, number rings, cones, non-commutative rings

title: Non-rational totally positive n in Q(√5): uncovered classes as a 'square obstruction' in O_K?
connection: other_rings: for D = 2, 5, 7, 13 some non-rational classes of (O_K/4)^* are not hit by the unit mechanism in the search box. Are these the square classes (a T1 analogue over K)?
why: If the missing classes are exactly squares mod 4O_K, T1 has a number-field generalization; if not, a new obstruction type exists.
first_step: Rerun scripts/bs_ff_rings.py for D = 5 with a larger box and compare the missing classes with the squares in (O_K/4)^*.
world: B. S-integers, number rings, cones, non-commutative rings

title: Eisenstein cone: Z[ω] with denominators in the 60° sector
connection: Z[ω] has 6 units; angular sectors are not closed under multiplication (arguments add), so a positive cone must be a semiring such as N-spans of a few units, or a sector cone with a weaker closure requirement. Each choice gives a different Eisenstein ES.
why: Choosing a closed cone in Z[ω] is itself a non-trivial design question that tests which positivity axioms matter.
first_step: Determine the multiplicatively closed cones in Z[ω] discrete at ∞ (e.g. N-span of {1, −ω²}?) and run the e-slice search in each.
world: B. S-integers, number rings, cones, non-commutative rings

title: Semiring cone Z_{≥0}[√2]: discrete at one real place, not at the other
connection: C = {a + b√2: a, b ≥ 0} ∖ {0} is multiplicatively closed, ≥ 1 at the identity embedding, but conjugates a − b√2 can be tiny. Intermediate between ℕ (fully discrete) and totally positive O_K (unit-rich).
why: Tests whether discreteness at ONE place suffices for hardness; if ES over this cone is again 'lottery', the archimedean crux is one-place.
first_step: Search the unit-sum mechanism in C: find e ∈ C, e ≡ 3 (mod 4O_K) with e = 1/u + 1/v, u, v ∈ C (note units 1+√2 ∈ C but (1+√2)^{-1} ∉ C).
world: B. S-integers, number rings, cones, non-commutative rings

title: Semiring cones Z_{≥0}[α] for α a Pisot or Salem number
connection: For α Pisot, Z_{≥0}[α] is discrete at the dominant place while conjugates shrink — like β-expansions. ES over these cones links to β-numeration (Pisot finiteness property F).
why: If ES-type statements over Z_{≥0}[α] relate to finiteness properties of β-expansions, there is a dynamical-systems literature to borrow.
first_step: Check the Frougny–Solomyak finiteness property (F) and test a numerator-4 ES in Z_{≥0}[golden ratio].
world: B. S-integers, number rings, cones, non-commutative rings

title: ES over Z[√−d] orders (non-maximal) with Gaussian-style cones
connection: Non-maximal orders (e.g. Z[2i], Z[√−3]) are not integrally closed; unit fractions behave differently at the conductor. ES for rational n in Z[2i] with Re, Im ≥ 0 sits between Z and Z[i].
why: Conductor primes give extra local constraints, a toy model of 'local obstruction at 2' that ES has with numerator 4.
first_step: Compare solution counts for rational p ≤ 10^4 in Z[i] vs Z[2i] cones.
world: B. S-integers, number rings, cones, non-commutative rings

title: Rational n in the Gaussian cone: is ES_Z[i](p) automatic for rational primes p ≡ 1 mod 4?
connection: Over Z[i], p = ππ̄ splits; 4/p = 4/(ππ̄) admits denominators built from π, giving many more divisors. Possibly the Gaussian cone ES for rational p is easy even though Conj. 1.1 for Gaussian primes is open.
why: If splitting makes rational p easy in the cone, the integer statement is 'ES with denominators x_i allowed to be Gaussian with positive parts' — a relaxation whose easiness is informative.
first_step: Brute force: for p ≡ 1 (mod 4) ≤ 10^4, find Gaussian-cone solutions using π-divisors; look for a uniform identity.
world: B. S-integers, number rings, cones, non-commutative rings

title: Hurwitz quaternions with positive-definite cone: non-commutative ES
connection: In a definite quaternion order, 1/x = x̄/N(x); require denominators with positive real part or in a cone. Non-commutativity gives more solutions per norm.
why: Quaternion norms connect ES to sums of four squares and Eichler orders; repo QUATERNION_ES treats an equivalent form — the cone version is a separate world.
first_step: Read QUATERNION_ES.md, then test 4/p = Σ 1/x_i with x_i Hurwitz quaternions of positive real part for p ≤ 1000.
world: B. S-integers, number rings, cones, non-commutative rings

title: Positive-definite integer matrices: (4/n)·I = X⁻¹ + Y⁻¹ + Z⁻¹
connection: In Sym_k(Z) with the positive-definite cone, diagonal solutions are k copies of ES; non-diagonal X allow far more freedom. For k = 2, is (4/n) I always a sum of three inverses of positive-definite integral matrices?
why: A proof via non-diagonal matrices would be a 'matrix ES' theorem; projecting back (e.g. by the (1,1) entry x₂₂/det X) gives 4/n as a sum of three fractions with structured numerators.
first_step: Search k = 2: enumerate positive-definite integral X with small entries and check whether (4/n)I − X⁻¹ − Y⁻¹ is the inverse of an integral PD matrix, for n = p ≤ 1000.
world: B. S-integers, number rings, cones, non-commutative rings

title: Matrix ES with commuting denominators reduces to number-field ES
connection: If X, Y, Z commute, they lie in a commutative order (a product of number-field orders), so matrix ES with commuting denominators ⇔ ES over products of orders with the totally-positive cone.
why: Shows the matrix world's novelty must come from non-commuting solutions; commuting ones are already covered by the number-field items.
first_step: State and prove the reduction (simultaneous diagonalization over Q-bar, positivity ↔ total positivity).
world: B. S-integers, number rings, cones, non-commutative rings

title: Group rings Z[C_m] with cone N[C_m]: ES in a ring with zero divisors
connection: Z[C_m] ≅ order in ∏ Q(ζ_d); the cone N[C_m] (non-negative coefficients) is multiplicatively closed and discrete in the trivial-character coordinate but not in others.
why: Combines several cyclotomic components with one positive coordinate; tests whether a single 'augmentation' coordinate carrying positivity suffices for hardness.
first_step: For m = 2 (Z[C_2] ≅ order in Q × Q), determine positive ES for n·1 and compare with ES over Z × Z.
world: B. S-integers, number rings, cones, non-commutative rings

title: Unit-sum mechanism over Z: the only integer e are 1 and 2 — consequence: classes 3 and 2 mod 4 only
connection: Over ℕ, 1/u + 1/v ∈ Z forces e ∈ {1, 2}, giving the classical easy classes. Any p-dependent replacement must produce e = 1/u + 1/v with u, v rational but with x = (n+e)/4 integer — i.e. e may depend on p.
why: Pins down the precise integer statement replacing the universal divisor: 'for every p there is e ≡ 3 mod 4 with e = 1/u+1/v and u·n·x, v·n·x integers' — which is ES itself in e-slice form.
first_step: Write the e-slice form explicitly and check it matches the repo's e-slice / Type I-II classification (ff Lemma 1.3 integer version).
world: B. S-integers, number rings, cones, non-commutative rings

title: Units of Z[1/2]: 4 becomes a unit and ES is trivial — the dyadic place carries the problem
connection: If 2 ∈ S the numerator 4 is a unit and ES collapses. Together with the Z[1/p] item: the obstruction is spread over the dyadic place and the place p.
why: Suggests a two-place reformulation: ES as a gluing problem between a 2-adic and a p-adic condition with an archimedean constraint.
first_step: Write ES as 'there exist local solutions at 2, p, ∞ with a common global lift of bounded height' and check it against STRONG_APPROX_ES.md.
world: B. S-integers, number rings, cones, non-commutative rings

title: Positive ES over Z[1/ℓ] with bounded ℓ-height: H_ℓ(p) := min over solutions of max ℓ-denominator
connection: Generalizing k(p) to all ℓ: H(p) = min over ℓ and solutions of ℓ^{depth}. ES ⇔ H(p) = 1. Which (ℓ, depth) are needed for the hardest primes?
why: A uniform bound like 'depth ≤ 1 for some ℓ ≤ 7' would be a clean new theorem target, perhaps reachable by the unit-sum mechanism with a p-dependent choice of ℓ.
first_step: Compute for p ≤ 10^6 the least (ℓ ≤ 50, depth) pair; histogram.
world: B. S-integers, number rings, cones, non-commutative rings

title: Archimedean crux restated as a 'gap principle' in valuation theory
connection: Cones discrete at all places where they carry sign (ℕ, monic F_q[T], Gaussian sector) give lottery problems; non-discrete cones collapse. Formalize: ES over (R, C) is a finite covering problem iff C ∩ {|x|_v < 1} ≠ ∅ for some sign place v.
why: A precise theorem of this kind would classify all analogue worlds at once and certify that Z is in the hard class.
first_step: State the theorem for Dedekind domains with a cone given by sign conditions at finitely many places; prove the 'collapse' direction from Lemma 3.1.
world: B. S-integers, number rings, cones, non-commutative rings

title: Imaginary quadratic fields with class number > 1: ES for principal vs non-principal primes
connection: Over O_K with h > 1, a rational prime p ≡ 1 mod 4 may split into non-principal primes; then 4/p has fewer 'divisor' options among principal elements. With a sector cone this is a new hard world.
why: Measures the role of class group in the divisor-in-class lottery; Z has h = 1.
first_step: Take K = Q(√−5), sector cone, test ES for rational p splitting into non-principal primes vs principal ones.
world: B. S-integers, number rings, cones, non-commutative rings

title: Positive ES over O_K for n ∈ O_K with Galois-conjugate denominators only
connection: Require the three denominators to form a Galois orbit (K cubic, x, σx, σ²x): 4/n = Tr(1/x). Then ES becomes 'n/4 is the reciprocal of a trace of a reciprocal' — a norm-form equation.
why: Gives a cubic norm-form reformulation for rational n: Tr_{K/Q}(1/x) = 4/n; such equations are amenable to Thue/Schmidt or to equidistribution of units.
first_step: For cyclic cubic K of small conductor, solve Tr(1/x) = 4/p for totally positive x ∈ O_K, p ≤ 10^4.
world: B. S-integers, number rings, cones, non-commutative rings

title: Integer ES solutions with x = Tr, y·z from norms: 'quadratic orbit' ES
connection: Variant: two denominators conjugate in a real quadratic field (y, ȳ) and one rational x: 4/n − 1/x = Tr(y)/N(y). Then ES ⇔ 4/n − 1/x is of the form a/b with a | b representable as (trace, norm) of a totally positive element — a binary quadratic form condition.
why: Converts ES into representation of numbers by binary quadratic forms with a trace constraint, linking to genus theory and class numbers (repo's CLASS_FORCING).
first_step: Make the equivalence explicit: 1/y + 1/ȳ = (y+ȳ)/(yȳ); classify which (t, N) arise and derive the binary-form condition.
world: B. S-integers, number rings, cones, non-commutative rings

title: Ring of algebraic integers Z-bar with totally positive cone: ES trivially true?
connection: In the ring of all algebraic integers, every element has square roots etc.; with a totally positive cone, the unit-sum mechanism has infinitely many units, so ES should collapse.
why: A sanity endpoint of the classification (infinite-degree world).
first_step: Note as corollary of Prop 3.3: Z-bar ⊃ Z[√2]; any rational n has a totally positive solution. Record.
world: B. S-integers, number rings, cones, non-commutative rings

title: p-adic integers with a 'sign' = class in Z_p^*/(Z_p^*)²: ES has local solutions always
connection: Z_p carries no order, but a sign can be a quadratic character. ES over Z_p with denominators in a quadratic-character cone is a local question solvable by Hensel; relevant only as local data.
why: Local data are inputs to Bright–Loughran's no-BM result and the singular series; the cone version records which sign patterns of x, y, z occur locally.
first_step: Compute, for ℓ ≤ 30, which (χ(x), χ(y), χ(z)) sign patterns occur for local solutions of 4/n with n ≡ 1 mod 4 — compare with global solutions' patterns.
world: B. S-integers, number rings, cones, non-commutative rings

title: Global sign patterns of ES solutions vs local predictions (Legendre symbols of x, y, z mod small primes)
connection: For each global solution record (x/ℓ), (y/ℓ), (z/ℓ). If some locally allowed pattern never occurs globally at hard primes, that is a hidden global constraint (reciprocity-type).
why: Hidden global constraints are exactly what T1 is; finding more of them maps the obstruction landscape.
first_step: Using existing solution data for p ≤ 10^6, tabulate patterns at ℓ = 3, 5, 7 and test against local frequencies.
world: B. S-integers, number rings, cones, non-commutative rings

title: Adelic ES: Bright–Loughran no Brauer–Manin obstruction ↔ strong approximation failure
connection: Integral points on the ES surface are not obstructed by Brauer–Manin; ES is therefore an 'existence of integral points beyond BM' question, like Markoff surfaces where strong approximation fails in a structured way.
why: Markoff surfaces have proven 'almost all' strong approximation (Bourgain–Gamburd–Sarnak, W. Chen); an analogous orbit structure on ES surfaces would be a transferable mechanism.
first_step: Check whether the ES affine surfaces have a nontrivial automorphism group acting on integral points (Vieta-like moves); see MARKOFF_ES.md.
world: B. S-integers, number rings, cones, non-commutative rings

title: Matrix ES over M₂(Z) with the cone of matrices with positive entries
connection: Matrices with positive entries form a multiplicatively closed cone discrete at ∞ (entries ≥ 1). Inverses are rational; ES: (4/n)·I = X⁻¹ + Y⁻¹ + Z⁻¹ with X, Y, Z positive-entry, invertible over Q.
why: This cone links ES to SL₂(N)-type monoids and continued fractions (the repo's SL₂ words form); it might reproduce ES exactly or relax it.
first_step: Check: does a solution with positive-entry X, Y, Z force a solution of ES? Compute small cases n = 5, 13, 17.
world: B. S-integers, number rings, cones, non-commutative rings

title: Matrix ES for n·I replaced by a matrix of determinant n
connection: Ask: for every integral M with det M = n (or Hermite normal form), is 4M⁻¹ = X⁻¹ + Y⁻¹ + Z⁻¹ with X, Y, Z positive-definite integral? For M = diag(1, n) it contains ES-like constraints in one coordinate.
why: Gives a family indexed by sublattices of index n; averaging over sublattices might be easier and still imply ES for M = n^{1/k}-free choices.
first_step: Work out k = 2, M = diag(1, p): what does positivity + integrality force on the (2,2) coordinate?
world: B. S-integers, number rings, cones, non-commutative rings

title: ES in Z × Z (product ring) with componentwise positivity: no coupling
connection: In a product ring ES holds iff it holds in each factor. Trivial, but it calibrates: coupling between places is what makes rings like O_K differ from Z × Z.
why: A boundary marker for the cone-classification theorem.
first_step: Note as a one-line lemma in the dictionary.
world: B. S-integers, number rings, cones, non-commutative rings

title: Real quadratic fields with N(ε) = +1: other_rings evidence shows coverage, find the proof

title: The numerator set M(p) is divisor-closed, so ES ⇔ M(p) contains a multiple of 4

title: Huang–Vaughan exceptional set asymptotic for a/n = 1/x+1/y → model for ES exceptions in a single slice
connection: Huang–Vaughan prove E_a(N) ~ C(a) N (log log N)^{2^{m−1}−1}/(log N)^{1−1/2^m} for fixed a, via 'delicate analysis of the underlying group structure' ((Z/aZ)^* and subgroups). ES needs a union over slices a = 4x − n with x varying.
why: Their group-structure analysis is exactly the 'divisor in a class' combinatorics; joint control over many a would be a quantitative almost-all ES with structure.
first_step: Read Huang–Vaughan's method and identify whether it extends to 'for some a in a set A(n)' with A depending on n (union bound + correlation).
world: C. Numerators m/n, k-term sums, constrained ES

title: One numerator-2 term trivializes ES: 4/n = 2/((n+1)/2) + 1/M + 1/M, M = n(n+1)/2
connection: For odd n: 4/n − 4/(n+1) = 4/(n(n+1)) = 2/M = 1/M + 1/M with M = n(n+1)/2. So allowing a single term with numerator 2 (and a repeat) solves every odd n.
why: Boundary marker: the 'weighted ES' world with weight vector (2,1,1) is trivial; difficulty is entirely in the all-ones weight vector.
first_step: Record as a lemma; then explore weight vectors (1,1,1) vs (1,1,2) vs (1,2,3) for distinct denominators.
world: C. Numerators m/n, k-term sums, constrained ES

title: Weighted ES: 4/n = a/x + b/y + c/z for fixed weight vectors (a,b,c)
connection: A whole family of ternary problems indexed by (a,b,c). (1,1,2) is trivial (previous item); (1,1,1) is ES. Which weight vectors are 'hard' (lottery) vs 'trivial' (identity covering) vs 'false'?
why: The hard/trivial boundary in weight space exposes what feature of (1,1,1) creates difficulty (e.g. no weight shares a factor with 4).
first_step: Brute-force n ≤ 10^4 for all (a,b,c) with a,b,c ≤ 4 and classify by existence of a finite covering by identities mod 840.
world: C. Numerators m/n, k-term sums, constrained ES

title: Signed ES with a size-controlled negative term: 4/n = 1/x + 1/y − 1/z with z ≥ n^{1+δ}
connection: Signed ES is trivial (4/(4k+1) = 1/k − 1/(k(4k+1))). Requiring the negative term to be tiny (z large) interpolates between trivial and ES-like. Find the threshold δ at which signed ES stops being covered by identities.
why: A threshold statement would be a new integer theorem halfway to ES, and the identity families near threshold are candidates to perturb into positive solutions.
first_step: For p ≤ 10^4, compute the maximal z over signed solutions with one negative term; check whether z ≥ p³ is always achievable (via identities).
world: C. Numerators m/n, k-term sums, constrained ES

title: Best underapproximation of 4/n by three unit fractions (Kovač / Nathanson / Chu) — ES ⇔ gap 0
connection: The 'best k-term underapproximation' literature studies max{Σ_{i≤k} 1/x_i ≤ q}. ES ⇔ the 3-term underapproximation of 4/n is exact. Structure theorems for best underapproximations (eventually greedy) might constrain when exactness is possible.
why: If best 3-term underapproximations of 4/n are 'eventually greedy' in a way that forces a particular x, ES reduces to a single e-slice — testable.
first_step: Read Kovač 2406.07218 and Nathanson 2202.00191; compute the best 3-term underapproximation of 4/p for p ≤ 10^4 and check whether greedy first term works.
world: C. Numerators m/n, k-term sums, constrained ES

title: Odd greedy algorithm (open termination problem) ↔ odd-denominator Egyptian fractions
connection: Every rational with odd denominator is a finite sum of distinct odd unit fractions (Breusch / Stewart, to check), but whether the odd greedy algorithm terminates is a famous open problem. ES with odd denominators is impossible (2-adic), but 4/n with an even number ≥ 4 of odd terms is a natural neighbour.
why: Two open problems about restricted Egyptian expansions; techniques from one (e.g. 2-adic descent) may cross over.
first_step: Check the status of the odd greedy problem and of 'minimal number of odd unit fractions for 4/n' (must be even ≥ 4 by parity); compute for n ≤ 1000.
world: C. Numerators m/n, k-term sums, constrained ES

title: Minimal number of odd unit fractions for 4/n: parity forces an even count ≥ 4
connection: A sum of k odd unit fractions has numerator Σ_i Π_{j≠i} x_j ≡ k (mod 2) over an odd denominator; since 4/n (n odd) has even numerator, k must be EVEN. Hence 4/n with odd denominators needs an even number of terms ≥ 4.
why: An odd-denominator 4-term ES ('4/n = four odd unit fractions') is a natural open-looking twin; study whether it is always solvable.
first_step: Compute for n ≤ 10^4 (n odd) whether 4/n is a sum of four odd unit fractions; look for obstructions mod 8.
world: C. Numerators m/n, k-term sums, constrained ES

title: Shifted-prime denominators (Bloom): 4/n with denominators of the form q − 1, q prime
connection: Bloom proved results on unit fractions with shifted prime denominators (density/Ramsey type). The 3-term restriction 4/n = Σ 1/(q_i − 1) is a sparse constrained world.
why: A sparse world where heuristics predict finitely many solutions overall tests the lottery model calibration (expected count ≪ 1 gives failures).
first_step: Compute the expected number of solutions under the lottery model and compare with brute force for n ≤ 10^4.
world: C. Numerators m/n, k-term sums, constrained ES

title: Semiprime denominators: 4/p as a sum of three reciprocals of semiprimes
connection: Recent work shows every natural number is a sum of distinct semiprime unit fractions (Shisheng Li). The 3-term version for 4/p is a constrained ES with a natural density of allowed denominators ~ log log x / log x.
why: Probes how ES's solution count scales when denominators are thinned to a density-zero but not too sparse set.
first_step: Brute force for p ≤ 10^4; record failure density; compare with lottery prediction.
world: C. Numerators m/n, k-term sums, constrained ES

title: Denominators in short intervals (Croot) ↔ size windows for ES solutions
connection: Croot studied unit fractions with denominators in short intervals [N, N + N^θ]. ES solutions have x ∈ (p/4, 3p/4] and y, z in structured ranges; asking for all three denominators in a short window is a size-constrained world.
why: Size windows are central to the repo's window/slice analysis; Croot's techniques give existence for long sums, hinting at what's needed for three.
first_step: Read Croot math/9904181 to see whether his argument has a 3-term component; compute the window widths of ES solutions for hard primes.
world: C. Numerators m/n, k-term sums, constrained ES

title: Rado/partition regularity of 1/x + 1/y + 1/z = 4/w
connection: Brown–Rödl-type results transfer Rado's theorem to reciprocal equations. Is 1/x + 1/y + 1/z = 4/w partition regular (monochromatic x, y, z, w in any finite colouring)? The linear counterpart x + y + z = 4w is not regular (no zero subset-sum of coefficients), but reciprocal equations can behave differently.
why: Partition regularity would be a robust 'many solutions' statement for the ES variety across all w, a Ramsey strengthening of 'ES has solutions'.
first_step: Check the reciprocal Rado literature (Brown–Rödl; Gaiser 2306.04029) for 1/x+1/y+1/z = c/w; try 2-colourings by computer for small ranges.
world: C. Numerators m/n, k-term sums, constrained ES

title: Covering systems ↔ unit fractions (Z.-W. Sun): ES as a statement about AP packings
connection: Sun relates m-covers by residue classes to sums of unit fractions of moduli. Three pairwise disjoint APs with moduli x, y, z have density Σ 1/x_i; ES ⇔ some disjoint triple of APs has density exactly 4/n (disjointness needs pairwise gcd > 1, which every ES solution has).
why: Imports covering-system technology (Hough, Balister–Bollobás–Morris–Sahasrabudhe–Tiba distortion method) into ES via packings.
first_step: Prove the equivalence 'ES ⇔ disjoint AP triple of density 4/n' and check whether every ES solution's moduli admit disjoint residues (pairwise gcd > 1 suffices).
world: C. Numerators m/n, k-term sums, constrained ES

title: Elsholtz–Planitzer approximate parametrizations for k ≥ 4 unit fractions
connection: For sums of four and more unit fractions, Elsholtz–Planitzer use approximate parametrizations to count solutions. ES is the k = 3 case where exact parametrizations (Type I/II) exist.
why: Their counting lower bounds for k ≥ 4 may have a pointwise version at specific n; a 4-term pointwise result plus a merging step would be a new route.
first_step: Read arXiv:2012.05984 and 1805.02945; check whether any pointwise (fixed n) 4-term statement is proved.
world: C. Numerators m/n, k-term sums, constrained ES

title: Four-term ES with distinct denominators is trivial — but four-term with a size cap is not
connection: 4/n as a sum of 4 unit fractions is easy (e.g. via 3/n splitting). With all denominators ≤ C·n (no huge denominators), the 4-term problem becomes a lattice/lottery problem again.
why: Size-capped multi-term ES might be provable for k = 4 with C large while ES (k = 3) remains open, giving a tunable intermediate theorem.
first_step: Compute, for n ≤ 10^4, the least C such that 4/n has a 4-term representation with max denominator ≤ C n; test boundedness.
world: C. Numerators m/n, k-term sums, constrained ES

title: Distinctness is harmless: the 'distinct' world never fails (p < 4000)
connection: Every p ≡ 1 mod 4 below 4000 has a solution with x, y, z distinct. Folklore says distinctness is WLOG for n > 2.
why: Confirms a reduction used everywhere; worth a one-line lemma (split a repeated term) to remove any doubt.
first_step: Write the splitting lemma: if x = y then 2/x = 1/(x/2)... or use 1/x = 1/(x+1) + 1/(x(x+1)) with care to keep 3 terms; check the literature statement.
refs: scripts/z52b_analogues_constraints.py (p ≡ 1 mod 4, p < 4000, all solutions enumerated)
world: C. Numerators m/n, k-term sums, constrained ES

title: A₃(p)-numerator geometry: the set M(p) as lattice points under a hyperbola
connection: m ∈ M(p) iff m/p = Σ 1/x_i; for each Type II parameter set, the achievable m form arithmetic progressions. M(p) is then a union of APs intersected with [1, 3p].
why: If M(p) is a union of many APs with differences coprime to 4, it contains a multiple of 4 — a pigeonhole route to ES via the numerator direction.
first_step: For p ≤ 10^4 compute M(p) and fit it as a union of APs; inspect the differences mod 4.
world: C. Numerators m/n, k-term sums, constrained ES

title: Egyptian fractions with restricted prime support (Chen–Elsholtz–Jiang; Czenky–McGovern–Plavnik)
connection: Representations of 1 with denominators in S(p_1,…,p_t) (S-units) are studied; ES in Z[1/S] relates. For ES over ℕ with denominators S-smooth except for factors of p, the count is finite and computable.
why: Gives an explicit finite-world version of ES (bounded prime support) where complete enumeration is possible and failure structure can be studied exactly.
first_step: For S = {2,3,5,7}, enumerate solutions of 4/p = Σ 1/x_i with x_i ∈ p^{0,1}·S-units, p ≤ 10^6; find which p are covered.
world: C. Numerators m/n, k-term sums, constrained ES

title: 4/n as a sum of three reciprocals of squares (Graham-type world)
connection: Graham characterized rationals that are finite sums of reciprocals of distinct squares. The 3-term version 4/n = 1/a² + 1/b² + 1/c² is a sparse world with local obstructions.
why: Not equivalent to ES, but a sibling in which local/global behaviour can be determined fully; it tests whether square-type obstructions come back with square denominators.
first_step: Compute for n ≤ 10^5 which n admit 4/n = Σ 1/a_i² (3 terms) and look for congruence patterns.
world: C. Numerators m/n, k-term sums, constrained ES

title: Mixed: 4/n = 1/x + 1/y + 1/z² (one square denominator)
connection: One square denominator keeps the problem 2-dimensional but couples to quadratic residues. It is a sibling where the T1 square obstruction might be amplified or cancelled.
why: If it is always solvable via an identity involving z² ≡ something, it gives a new certificate type over Z.
first_step: Brute force n ≤ 10^4; for each solvable n record the class of z mod small primes.
world: C. Numerators m/n, k-term sums, constrained ES

title: ES with denominators restricted to a numerical semigroup or to values of a polynomial
connection: E.g. denominators of the form k(k+1) (pronic) telescope: 1/(k(k+1)) = 1/k − 1/(k+1). ES with pronic denominators is a strongly restricted world with a telescoping algebra.
why: Telescoping algebras convert sums into differences, i.e. into signed problems; the pronic world might be equivalent to a signed ES with special structure.
first_step: Brute force n ≤ 10^4 for pronic and triangular denominators; derive the equivalence with signed sums.
world: C. Numerators m/n, k-term sums, constrained ES

title: Distinct-odd unit fraction representations: every odd-denominator rational is a finite sum (to check: Breusch 1954, Stewart 1954)
connection: If verified, this is the 'unbounded-length odd' world where existence is known; ES's length-3 even-structured requirement is the opposite extreme.
why: Their proofs (greedy variants with parity) may give length bounds for 4/n with odd terms, a quantitative statement between the worlds.
first_step: Check whether Breusch/Stewart give explicit length bounds; compute minimal odd lengths for 4/n, n ≤ 1000.
world: C. Numerators m/n, k-term sums, constrained ES

title: Rational numbers representable with three unit fractions: density among a/b with b ≤ N
connection: Most rationals a/b with a large are not 3-term sums. ES says all 4/n are. Placing 4/n in the 2D picture (a, b) shows ES is on a 'ray' where the density is 1 conjecturally.
why: If density along the ray a = 4 is provably 1 (Vaughan) and along a = c log b provably 0, the transition curve is a precise target for heuristics.
first_step: Compute, for b ≤ 2000, the proportion of representable a/b as a function of a; plot transition.
world: C. Numerators m/n, k-term sums, constrained ES

title: ES restricted to 'Type I only' or 'Type II only': two sub-worlds with known almost-all behaviour
connection: Elsholtz–Tao distinguish Type I (p divides one denominator) and Type II (p divides two). Each sub-world is a constrained ES; which primes need Type II? (Computation: 'y, z both divisible by p' never fails below 4000; 'only z divisible by p' never fails either.)
why: Since both sub-worlds appear complete numerically, each is a strengthening of ES and may be easier to attack structurally (one family of divisor conditions).
first_step: Extend to 10^6: does 'Type II only' (p | y, p | z) ever fail? (Repo has censuses—check I3/Type II data first.)
refs: scripts/z52b_analogues_constraints.py (p ≡ 1 mod 4, p < 4000, all solutions enumerated)
world: C. Numerators m/n, k-term sums, constrained ES

title: Greedy/Fibonacci–Sylvester world: 4/n has ≤ 4 greedy terms; ES needs 3
connection: The greedy algorithm on 4/n terminates in at most 4 terms (numerators decrease). The classes where greedy gives 3 terms are covered; ES fails for greedy at others but other expansions work.
why: Greedy-type deterministic algorithms with a 'look-ahead' choice might reach 3 terms always — an algorithmic proof template.
first_step: Implement 'greedy with first term chosen from {⌈n/4⌉ + j : j ≤ J}' and find the least J(p) for which the remainder is a 2-term sum; study J(p) growth.
world: C. Numerators m/n, k-term sums, constrained ES

title: ES for numerators m that are prime vs composite (4 composite, 5 prime)
connection: Divisor-closure links composite numerators to their divisors; a prime numerator m has no proper non-trivial divisor (except 1). Compare exception structures across prime and composite m.
why: If composite m are systematically 'easier' through factor structure, the integer statement 'ES(4) ⇐ ES(2)-type subproblems' may have a useful partial version.
first_step: Using the Schinzel table item, compare exception counts for m prime vs composite at fixed n-range.
world: C. Numerators m/n, k-term sums, constrained ES

title: Egyptian fractions on topological groups (Ross): ES in the circle group or in Q_p
connection: Ross extends structure results on sets of Egyptian fractions to subsets of topological groups. An ES analogue in R/Z or Q_p asks which elements are 3-term sums from a discrete generating set.
why: Topological closures of the set of 3-term sums (accumulation points are 2-term sums, etc.) give a 'derived set' picture; ES points must avoid being only limit points.
first_step: Read arXiv:2410.24165 to see which structure theorems carry over and whether derived-set orders give constraints on 4/n.
world: C. Numerators m/n, k-term sums, constrained ES

title: Derived-set (accumulation) structure: 4/n is never an accumulation point of 3-term sums except via 2-term limits
connection: The set E₃ of 3-term sums is closed with accumulation points in E₂ (2-term sums). 4/n ∈ E₃ is a statement about an isolated vs limit point.
why: If 4/n lies in the closure of E₃ for trivial reasons (approximations from above/below), quantifying the approximation rate may force membership for arithmetic reasons.
first_step: Compute dist(4/p, E₃ ∖ {4/p}) for p ≤ 10^4 and compare with the expected spacing.
world: C. Numerators m/n, k-term sums, constrained ES

title: Engel and Pierce expansions: ES as a length-3 Engel-type representation
connection: Chain solutions (x | y | z) are Engel-like (1/x(1 + 1/a(1 + 1/b))). Engel/Pierce expansions of 4/n are deterministic; their lengths give a dynamical invariant.
why: If a variant of Engel expansion of 4/n always has length ≤ 3 after a single 'reset', ES follows; computing it is cheap.
first_step: Compute the Engel expansion length of 4/p for p ≤ 10^5; correlate with chain-world failures (38 below 4000).
refs: scripts/z52b_analogues_constraints.py (p ≡ 1 mod 4, p < 4000, all solutions enumerated)
world: C. Numerators m/n, k-term sums, constrained ES

title: Triangle orbifolds: ES ⇔ 4/n − 1 is the Euler characteristic of a turnover S²(x,y,z)
connection: χ^orb(S²(x,y,z)) = 1/x + 1/y + 1/z − 1. So ES(n) ⇔ some hyperbolic triangle orbifold has χ = (4 − n)/n, i.e. area 2π(1 − 4/n).
why: Moves ES into the world of triangle groups Δ(x,y,z), where finite-index subgroups, Riemann–Hurwitz and arithmeticity (Takeuchi's list) give structure; e.g. a torsion-free subgroup of index d has 2g − 2 = d(n − 4)/n.
first_step: Check whether 'areas of hyperbolic triangle orbifolds' as a set of rationals has been studied (search 'orbifold Euler characteristic triangle group which rationals'); list areas for arithmetic triangle groups.
world: D. Geometric, topological and combinatorial host worlds

title: Riemann–Hurwitz integrality: a surface subgroup of Δ(x,y,z) of index d needs n | d(n − 4)
connection: For an ES solution, a torsion-free normal subgroup of index d in Δ(x,y,z) yields genus g with 2g − 2 = d(1 − 4/n). Hence n must divide d(n − 4); for prime n ≥ 5 this forces n | d.
why: Translates ES into 'Δ(x,y,z) has a finite quotient of order divisible by n with x, y, z element orders' — a group-theoretic existence statement where e.g. PSL₂(F_q) quotients (Macbeath) are classified.
first_step: For small n list ES triples and check whether PSL₂(F_p) is a quotient of Δ(x,y,z) (Macbeath's criterion); see if a uniform choice like PSL₂(F_p) suggests a construction.
world: D. Geometric, topological and combinatorial host worlds

title: Brieskorn–Pham log canonical thresholds: ES ⇔ 4/n = lct(x^a + y^b + z^c)
connection: For the diagonal singularity x^a + y^b + z^c, lct = min(1, 1/a + 1/b + 1/c). So ES(n) ⇔ 4/n (< 1 for n ≥ 5) is the log canonical threshold of a 3-variable Brieskorn–Pham polynomial.
why: Birational geometry studies the set LCT₃ of 3-dimensional lcts (ACC, accumulation points); ES asks whether all 4/n lie in the Brieskorn–Pham stratum. Other quasi-homogeneous types give natural relaxations.
first_step: Check the known description of LCT for quasi-homogeneous isolated singularities in 3 variables (Arnold's types) and list which rationals arise from each type.
world: D. Geometric, topological and combinatorial host worlds

title: Quasi-homogeneous relaxations: lct of x^a y + y^b + z^c is (a + b − 1)/(ab) + 1/c
connection: For f = x^a y + y^b + z^c, weights w_y = 1/b, w_x = (b − 1)/(ab), w_z = 1/c give lct = Σ w = (a+b−1)/(ab) + 1/c (if ≤ 1). Each Arnold/Orlik–Wagreich type gives a 'generalized Egyptian' expression for rationals.
why: A family of ES-like problems with a geometric origin; if one type (e.g. chain x^a y + y^b z + z^c) represents every 4/n, it is a provable relaxation and its proof might be adapted.
first_step: Derive the weight-sum formulas for the 7 Orlik–Wagreich-type classes of 3-variable isolated quasi-homogeneous singularities and test which represent 4/p for all p ≤ 10^4.
world: D. Geometric, topological and combinatorial host worlds

title: Brieskorn links: ES solutions never give integral homology spheres
connection: The link of x^a + y^b + z^c is an integral homology sphere iff a, b, c are pairwise coprime. Pairwise coprime ES solutions are impossible (constraint-world item), so ES links always have non-trivial H₁.
why: Gives a topological invariant (H₁ of the link, related to gcds of the denominators) attached to every solution; the gcd skeleton of Type I/II solutions becomes the torsion of H₁.
first_step: Compute H₁ of Brieskorn links for ES triples of small p and compare with the Type I/II parameters.
world: D. Geometric, topological and combinatorial host worlds

title: Seifert fibred spaces: ES ⇔ M(0; (x,1), (y,1), (z,1)) has rational Euler number −4/n
connection: For a Seifert space over S² with unnormalized invariants (α_i, β_i) = (x_i, 1) and b = 0, e = −Σ β_i/α_i = −(1/x + 1/y + 1/z). So ES ⇔ such a space has e = −4/n, and then |H₁| = xyz·|e| = 4xyz/n = xy + yz + zx.
why: Seifert spaces with given e are related by Dehn surgery and covers; covering a solution space by another gives multiplicative maps between ES problems (degree-d covers scale e).
first_step: Check: a fibre-preserving d-fold cover of M multiplies e by a rational factor; derive which covers map ES(n) solutions to ES(n') solutions.
world: D. Geometric, topological and combinatorial host worlds

title: Pretzel links: det P(x,y,z) = xy + yz + zx = 4xyz/n for ES triples
connection: The pretzel link P(x,y,z) has determinant |xy + yz + zx| (its double branched cover is the Seifert space above). ES ⇔ some pretzel link with positive parameters has det·n = 4·xyz.
why: Knot-theoretic invariants of pretzel links (Alexander polynomial, signature, Heegaard Floer d-invariants) give new numerical invariants of ES solutions to correlate with hardness.
first_step: For ES triples of small p compute signature and Alexander polynomial of P(x,y,z); look for constraints that would forbid solutions at specific p.
world: D. Geometric, topological and combinatorial host worlds

title: Star-shaped Dynkin trees T_{x,y,z}: det(Cartan) = xyz(1/x + 1/y + 1/z − 1)
connection: The tree T_{p,q,r} (arms with p, q, r vertices including the centre) has Cartan determinant pqr(1/p+1/q+1/r − 1) (E₈ = T_{2,3,5}: 1; E₆ = T_{2,3,3}: 3). ES ⇔ some T_{x,y,z} has n·det = xyz(4 − n), a hyperbolic lattice of discriminant xyz(n−4)/n.
why: Brings in lattice/root-system tools (discriminant groups, Vinberg reflectivity) and the recent weighted-star-tree classification of Torrente-Lujan.
first_step: Compute discriminant groups of T_{x,y,z} lattices for ES triples of small p; see whether they have a uniform structure (e.g. cyclic of order xyz(n−4)/n).
world: D. Geometric, topological and combinatorial host worlds

title: Weighted star trees with central weight k: generalized ES 4/n = 1/x + 1/y + 1/z − (k − 2)
connection: Torrente-Lujan allows central diagonal entry k; the determinant becomes xyz(Σ 1/x_i − (k − 1)) up to normalization (check the exact formula). Different k shift the target by integers, giving 'ES with integer offset'.
why: Integer offsets are trivial arithmetically but the matrix world might impose inertia/definiteness constraints that select ES-relevant triples.
first_step: Read arXiv:2605.23011 for the determinant formula with general k and record the induced Egyptian equation.
world: D. Geometric, topological and combinatorial host worlds

title: Parallel resistors: ES ⇔ a resistance n/4 Ω made from three integer resistors in parallel
connection: Conductances add in parallel: 1/R = 1/x + 1/y + 1/z. So ES ⇔ R = n/4 is a parallel combination of three integer resistors (equivalently three thin lenses of integer focal length in contact).
why: Electrical networks connect to squared rectangles (Brooks–Smith–Stone–Tutte) and Kirchhoff matrix-tree counts; a network-theoretic proof of a 'three-branch' realizability statement is conceivable.
first_step: Check the literature on 'realizing resistance values with k resistors' (series–parallel, minimal number of unit resistors) for 3-branch parallel results.
world: D. Geometric, topological and combinatorial host worlds

title: Rectangle tilings: ES ⇔ an n×4 rectangle split into three horizontal strips, each a row of equal squares
connection: A strip of width W tiled by x equal squares has height W/x; three strips stacked give height W(1/x+1/y+1/z). Thus ES(n) ⇔ the rectangle of aspect n : 4 is tiled by three such strips.
why: Tiling theory (Dehn's theorem, Laczkovich–Szekeres tilings with similar rectangles) studies which aspect ratios are tileable under constraints; ES is a 3-strip constrained tiling.
first_step: Formalize and check whether allowing strips to be split further (two-level tilings) yields a known Dehn-type characterization that ES is a restriction of.
world: D. Geometric, topological and combinatorial host worlds

title: Perfectly periodic schedules: three tasks with periods x, y, z sharing a slot pattern of density 4/n
connection: A perfectly periodic schedule assigns task i to an AP of period x_i, all disjoint. ES ⇔ three disjoint APs of total density 4/n exist. Pinwheel scheduling (Kawamura: density threshold 5/6 proved) studies the non-exact version.
why: Scheduling algorithms (and their impossibility certificates) are a new source of combinatorial tools for disjoint-AP packings with prescribed density.
first_step: Read Kawamura's density-threshold proof to see if exact-density perfectly periodic schedules with three tasks are characterized.
world: D. Geometric, topological and combinatorial host worlds

title: Kraft–McMillan / compact trees ↔ sums of unit fractions (Elsholtz–Heuberger–Prodinger)
connection: Compact prefix codes and canonical trees are counted via sums of unit fractions; ES-type identities appear as specific tree shapes with three leaves of weights 1/x_i summing to 4/n.
why: A tree/code interpretation may give a bijective or generating-function handle on solution counts.
first_step: Read arXiv:1108.5964 to see which unit-fraction equations correspond to which trees; check whether 3-leaf subtrees encode ES.
world: D. Geometric, topological and combinatorial host worlds

title: Landau's class equation and fusion-category Egyptian equations: 1 = Σ 1/|C(g_i)|
connection: Integral modular categories and finite groups yield Egyptian equations for 1 (Landau; Bruillard–Rowell). A group with 4 conjugacy classes gives 1 − 1/|G| = three unit fractions, an ES-type equation with numerator |G| − 1.
why: Shows ES-like equations arising from algebraic structures where existence is guaranteed by constructions; the analogous numerator family (N−1)/N is a sibling world.
first_step: Enumerate (N−1)/N = 1/a + 1/b + 1/c solutions and compare with groups having 4 classes (Z₄, V₄, D₅, A₄); note which equations are 'realized'.
world: D. Geometric, topological and combinatorial host worlds

why: If the FF-Gaussian twin is proved (by FF methods) while the Z-Gaussian twin is open, the transfer gap is the same as for ES — confirming the gap is archimedean, not about i.
first_step: Define the sign function on F_q[T][√D] for D of odd degree (imaginary quadratic FF) and run the e-slice search.
world: G. Invented worlds, p-dependent fields, integer-side replacement statements
